utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Manning, do I correctly understand that you may wish to respond to Mr. Ivetic's revised request to extend the areas into which -- on which you may cross-examine?

utterances.speaker: MS. MANNING
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell me, then, what you wish to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. MANNING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for providing the US Government an opportunity to respond directly to Mr. Lukic's request for assistance. Given the break in testimony, the United States Government has had the opportunity to consider, on an expedited basis, Mr. Lukic's revised request of April 12th to expand the scope of cross-examination in response to each of the listed points as follows: With respect to point A, the US Government authorises the cross-examination of Mr. Byrnes on the meetings Mr. Byrnes and the US Government officials had with the KLA during his time in Kosovo. With respect to point B, the US Government does not comment on alleged intelligence matters, and thus similarly declines to do so in this context. We also note our agreement with the Prosecution's comments from yesterday that this topic is not relevant to the issues on which Mr. Byrnes is testifying. With respect to point C, the US Government authorises cross-examination of Mr. Byrnes on his service with US KDOM and his other relevant Balkans experience. Finally, with respect to point D, this is not an issue so much as an allegation. Mr. Byrnes was in Kosovo as head of the US Kosovo diplomatic observer mission established pursuant to the US Security Council resolution 1199. To the extent that the Defence wishes to cross-examine Mr. Byrnes on his activities with US KDOM, the US has already authorised this pursuant to C. Thus with this last comment, the US Government has completed its response to Defence counsels' revised request dated April 12th. As one final point, we would want to inform the parties that the US Embassy received Mr. Ivetic's original April 12th request yesterday afternoon, which is consistent with our experience that the registry filings generally require two to three business days for delivery. Thus, we appreciate Judge Bonomy's noting that the proper channel of communication for a request to a State is directly to that State. Direct communication not only avoids delays and confusion, but, important to Defence counsel, preserves the confidentiality of a request. Thus, we would request parties to contact us directly, either here in The Hague at the office of legal counsel at the US Embassy or with relevant authorities in Washington. Again, the US Government extends its thank you and its appreciation to the court for the opportunity to be heard on these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Manning. Mr. Ivetic, I think that what's just been said confirming the indication given by the Court yesterday that the appropriate and speedier way of dealing with this sort of thing is directly between party and state is a point to be noted generally, and indeed there's the additional point now made that filing may actually be inappropriate. However, when we get to this stage and a response has been given orally to a written filing, then to make sense of the response it's necessary to have -- to a written document, it's necessary to have that document filed. So that document, that revised request, will now have to be filed. And it should be filed along with the -- although you delivered the original request, I don't think it was necessarily filed by the registry. I think both should now be filed in the context of this case. Is there something else you would like to say now in relation to the response?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to seek clarification with respect to any questions aimed at points -- at the points that were allowed. Do those need to be in closed session or open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Manning.

utterances.speaker: MS. MANNING
utterances.text: Open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We can have the witness back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we've delayed you a little again, but there were administrative issues to be clarified. These have now been dealt with. It simply falls for me to remind you that the solemn declaration -- you're hearing nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The workers muscle us from time to time. The only thing I have to do before your cross-examination resumes is to remind you that the solemn declaration which you gave at the beginning of your evidence, to speak the truth continuous, to apply to that evidence until it is concluded. The cross-examination by Mr. Ivetic will now continue. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Byrnes. As I promised yesterday, we'll hopefully be brief. I only have about 15 or 20 questions for you, so we'll get right started. Now, I want to clarify one thing from yesterday. I believe you stated yesterday that you did not remember if you discussed with Mr. Lukic anything about 30.000 [Realtime transcript read in error as "30"] long-barrelled weapons having been brought into Kosovo from Albania by the KLA. Irrespective of whether you had a discussion with Mr. Lukic or not, do you recall having any such information at any point in time when you were deployed as part of US KDOM?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, just one moment. Yesterday, it was 30.000 long-barrelled weapons, and it's now 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 30.000, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 30.000, okay. Only those - well, including you - with the benefit of the transcript in front of them, can see the funny side, but we now have the 30.000 recorded.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I distinctly remember he used the term 30.000 yesterday, and that's what I heard him -- Mr. Ivetic say today. In response to his question, let me repeat. I honestly have no recollection of using that figure in a discussion with General Lukic. As I said earlier, I had many, many, many discussions with General Lukic over the course of my mandate in Kosovo. I would like to make two further points, and then a third, if I may, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can try to just get an answer to the question first. Do you know about 30.000 weapons -- 30.000 long-barrelled weapons being brought in by the KLA? That's really the gist of my question.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I add -- may I add something, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you feel it's necessary to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was common knowledge in Kosovo among the internationals serving there, and I'm certain certainly among the Serbian security forces, that the KLA was smuggling weapons from Albania into Kosovo before, during and after the October agreement. And if I may add an anecdote, I was told once by one of the Llap zone commander, Polijevo zone commander, Remi, that he on occasion was purchasing weapons from a Yugoslav Army colonel based in Nis, and that these weapons would come down to his positions in Yugoslav army trucks at night. I cannot confirm that, but I think it's worth passing on. Finally, I do recall having conversations with General Lukic about the problem of the smuggling of weapons by the KLA into Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transcript probably should show on 6.4, and that might be changed without me doing anything, but it looks like the weapons are coming from France; they're actually from Nis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Hopefully the rest of the questions in this cross will go a little easier with the transcript than they have thus far.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we're on Commander Remi and the Llap's commands out of the KLA, did you also have occasion to contact -- to have contact with Mr. Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never did personally. Let me add, people in our mission who were based in Pec, where we had an outstation, did have contact Haradinaj. I never did personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's important to have the names correct, and at line 6.3, I believe it Remi, R-e-m-i, and at line 16, it should be Ramush, not Remush.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. So far we're three for three. Let's try another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With respect to the contacts that your US KDOM personnel had with Mr. Haradinaj, did you have knowledge of any of his admissions as to having killed dozens of persons with his own hands?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I did not and we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you yesterday described another KLA officer, I think it's Geci, G-e-c-i, and you mentioned that he was an unsavoury, sinister character. Did you pass along this kind of information about the criminal nature of the KLA back through your diplomatic channels to the authorities in the United States?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I'm waiting for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's another transcript error that's significant. If we could go back to page 5, line -- I think it's page 5, line 24 -- line 25, it says the KLA was smuggling weapons into Albania from Kosovo. It's the opposite of that. It was into Kosovo from Albania, and that's an important difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's important also to remember that this is the initial transcript which is then -- well, which is then revised in light of listening to the tapes, and most of these matters are resolved. But it's helpful to have noted the various ones that are occurring today. We'll continue to monitor the transcript closely. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Byrnes, despite having information from yourself and others in the field as to the criminal nature of some of the commanders of the KLA, was there still pressure from Washington to at least downplay the KLA activities if not assist them to put pressure on the Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was not, and I would be happy to amplify that if the Court felt that would be necessary and important.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You've answered my question. That's all I had to ask about that. To your knowledge, did --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Byrnes, it ought to be made clear that in cross-examination, the control of the questioning lies in the hands of the examiner. However, you must be given every opportunity to ensure that you've given a full answer to the question. But if what's involved is supplementary information rather than a full answer or clarification of the answer, then it's really a matter that the Prosecution can raise with you if they wish to later, and also Mr. Ivetic, if he really wants that information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And may I ask you a question on this sort of issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This refers to testimony yesterday. I was asked -- I was asked several what I consider quite general questions about the situation in Kosovo after the October agreements were signed, and I found -- you may have noticed, I found them difficult to answer because of their generality. I thought a good deal about that overnight, and my own feeling is it would be useful to amplify those in a general way. I think in doing so, I could provide or I would certainly like to provide a better picture of what I saw in Kosovo during the period in question. I don't know if, that's up to you or the Defence or the Prosecution, but I feel it would be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what you've done is alert all the parties to the availability of additional information, and Mr. Hannis will have a chance to re-examine you. If, following that, we feel it's necessary to explore the matter further, then we'll do so from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Byrnes, to your knowledge, did the KLA receive satellite telephones from the US KDOM or KVM?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. I think this is beyond the scope of the direct examination and anything additional that was allowed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I can withdraw the question and go into specifics, if it's much easier, Your Honour. I think it will move this along a lot quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you think that can be done, we'll come back, if it remains a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you now about some of the contacts you had with the KLA, Mr. Byrnes. Do you recall travelling to Krajmirovci and Sedlare villages on the 15th of February, 1999 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm being urged to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall travelling to Krajmirovci and Sedlare, S-e-d-l-a-r-e, villages on the 15th of February, 1999, to meet with KLA commanders Fatim Sedlare, F-a-t-i-m S-e-d-l-a-r-e, Heset Sahiti, H-e-s-e-t S-a-h-i-t-i, and Rudzi Buja, R-u-d-z-i B-u-j-a, among others, where you reviewed their 121st Brigade and reassured them publicly that despite the Serbian delegation in France not wanting to give up Kosovo, that the United States would do everything within its power to get the Albanians what had been promised to them before the negotiations? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know of any promises that have been made to the Albanians prior to the negotiations in France?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No promises were made to the Albanians by our special negotiator, Chris Hill. His task was to try to sell the Albanians essentially on greater autonomy within Serbia, within Federal Yugoslavia, at least, and that was the backbone and core of the Rambouillet agreement. We were, of course, fully aware that the KLA and, I would add, Mr. Rugova's LDK aim was full independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you, on the 13th of February, 1999, meet with these various KLA commanders?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fifteenth, Your Honour, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry? Which--

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fifteenth is what I have in my notes, but the transcript shows the 13th. Well, any time from the 13th through the 15th.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- to be honest, I have no idea at this point, nine years later, where I was on the 13th or 15th. Secondly, the names of the three KLA officers that were brought up and that I see on my screen do not -- do not ring any bells. I don't remember meeting anybody with those names.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall reviewing the units of the 121st Brigade of the KLA at any time in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not, and I'd like to add for the record that when we met with KLA commanders in the field, they were extremely reticent about identifying their units. We rarely were told what the unit number was or the units name were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you about December of 1998. Do you recall passing a message directly from Washington to Mahmuti Bardhyl, through your translator -- your personal translator, Mr. Jare, following the abduction and killing of Kosovo Polje's deputy prefect in which the United States stressed that the KLA needed to condemn the killing and work to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- and work to improve its image because its actions in taking over Serb positions were making it difficult for General Clark to justify NATO air strikes against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, this is working badly today, I'm afraid. We're going to have to slow right down for reasons which are not clear to me at the moment. And there is already something missing from that question, because I think I heard reference to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a reference to the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second, just a second, Mr. Hannis, in which the United States stressed they needed to -- what was the rest of that part?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That the KLA needed to condemn the killing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had an objection regarding the foundation for this question. It doesn't appear to arise from his interview notes, which are something -- if that's what it's coming from, we should go into closed session. But if it's not, I don't know what the foundation is. If it's a document that I've been provided, if Mr. Ivetic could tell me which one it is, I could refer to it. But these are very specific questions, and I don't know what the foundation for them is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The foundation for my prior question was 6206, official notes of the state security services that were monitoring Mr. Byrnes. The second one is -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the reference to the Exhibit was 6D-206. MR: IVETIC: That is correct, Your Honour, and the question that I have now posed comes out of 6D-202, operative information of the sector for state security, the DB centre in Pristina dated January the 6th, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you quote again the number of the latter exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. The second exhibit is 6D, as in David, 202, 6D-202.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I have is an English translation of the document. It's titled "Official Note" and purportedly from the Ministry of Foreign affairs, but there is no signature nor stamp. I don't know what the provenance of this is. It could have been typed up anywhere, any time. So I have a question about the good-faith basis of the question without knowing something more about the provenance of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, Mr. Hannis, the question that relates to the direct personal knowledge of the witness, and there is an ostensible basis for it, and indeed, an assurance from counsel that he has such a basis. What can your objection be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this could come from anywhere. This could have been pulled off the internet by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. So the way to clarify it is to ask the witness, surely. It's not as if he -- Mr. Ivetic is making it up. Someone else may. That's a matter you can deal with. But surely when it's a matter of the personal knowledge of the witness, it's legitimate for him to ask the witness his position on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure how it relates to the personal knowledge of the witness. This is supposedly, I guess, an intercept that is claimed to have been taken regarding Mr. Byrnes as a speaker. But what's the prominence or authenticity for that? How do we know that a person listening knows who Mr. Byrnes was or what his voice sounds like?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a matter you'll be able to deal with if there is an attempt made by the Defence to present that as positive evidence in their case, but all that's happening at the moment is that questions are being asked. You sought an indication of the foundation, and the foundation has been intimated to you, and we are satisfied that it is appropriate for these questions to be asked on that basis. So please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I guess to be fair to the witness and to the transcript, I should repeat the question now, since we've gone far afield from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, do you recall, in December of 1998, passing a message from Washington to Mr. Mahmuti Bardhyl or Bardhyl Mahmuti? Bardhyl is B-a-r-d-u-l-j [sic], Mahmuti, M-a-h-m-u-t-i-j-a [sic], who I believe was the KLA officer for -- liaison officer for affairs with the Diaspora. Mahmuti should be M-a-h-m-u-t-i, and Bardhyl should be B-a-r-d-h-y-l. I apologise. The KLA liaison officer for the Diaspora, and this message was supposed to have been relayed by you through your personal translator, Mr. Valin Dezar [phoen], following the abduction and killing of Kosovo's deputy prefect, Mr. Bojanic, in which the United States stressed that the KLA needed to, first, condemn the killing and then work to improve its image because its actions, including the taking over of Serb positions, was making it difficult for General Clark to justify air strikes against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. And I would like to amplify my comments or my response. First, I did have contact by cellphone with Mr. Mahmuti. Second, the name Valin Dezar is one I have never, ever heard of. My personal translator was a woman named Florina Krasnici. When I spoke with Mr. Mahmuti, I spoke directly with him in Serbian. He spoke excellent Serbian. I did not require the services of a translator. And, finally, the point I would like to make is the United States Government at that time was deeply interested and intensively engaged in trying to find a political resolution to this crisis. The last thing that the Clinton administration wanted - and I know personally Christopher Hill, who was a special envoy and with whom I worked closely - wanted was more conflict and more trouble with Serbia. The United States had enjoyed traditionally historically excellent relations with Serbia, dating back to our consular agreement in 1881. We had been close allies in World War I and World War II, and we wanted to restore our traditional relationships. We did not want to bomb. We were doing everything we could to avoid that, that event, that consequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if I can move on. Yesterday, you described an operation, I believe, near Pec in September of 1998, and I believe the village involved was Istinic, I-s-t-i-n-i-c, where you stated that the police attacked the villages, believing them to be harbouring the KLA, and forced people from those villages before forcing them back. Am I correct that you did not personally eyewitness this event?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise again. I'm waiting for the transcript. All right, sir. Now, did your US KDOM personnel that were present at the scene, did they speak with any of the senior MUP officers present during the whole operation, such as, for example, Assistant-Minister General Obrad Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of that, unfortunately. No, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Did you receive information that, in fact, civilians were not only permitted to return to their homes in the village, but that they were also permitted to go anywhere else they desired, and that a fair number of persons went to Pec and to the municipality of Djakovica of their own volition?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our teams reported that a number of the displaced Albanians did not return to their villages because they had nothing to return to. Their homes had been destroyed, and so they went to relatives or friends in Pec or Djakovica or other villages nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you receive information that there were even some KLA members mixed in among the civilians who were permitted to go wherever they desired as well?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received no specific information that there were KLA members mixed in, but in the interests of truth I would add that we -- my team and I personally strongly suspected, given -- given the type of insurgency that was going on, that there probably were KLA members who were seeking to escape Serbian encirclement by posing as civilians, but I had no direct knowledge of that, nor did my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, another important factor for this incident that I want to ask you about is: Did you have knowledge or were you aware that several members of the Red Cross were instructing villagers not to go back to their homes and were otherwise causing panic among the masses? Here I'm talking about Ms. Ann Dellforge [phoen] and her associates who had previously run afoul of the authorities by transporting illegal radio equipment in the area?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no recollection of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Now, just briefly dealing with the MUP itself, I presume you are aware that the MUP was divided into two sectors; one for public safety and one for state security.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And were you also aware that the state security or the RDB had a chain of communication and command separate and apart from the public safety sector?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, at least for me, there was some confusion as to when the US KDOM mission left Kosovo. I guess the easiest way for me to clarify it is: Do you recall if yourself and the rest of the KDOM personnel left Kosovo before NATO started the air campaign?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very definitely, all the KDOMs and KDM left Kosovo before the air campaign began. Very definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that clarifies it for my purposes. I have just one more question. With respect to the RJB, the public safety sector of the MUP, am I correct that you have no direct information as to how this sector functioned after the declaration of war, that is to say, after NATO started bombing, or who the most senior MUP officers on the ground were during that time?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Byrnes. I'm all finished questioning you. I apologise for the fact it took a little longer than we had anticipated. Thank you for your assistance. Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, I have a handful of questions for you on redirect. Yesterday, Mr. Fila asked you some questions about your conversations with Mr. Sainovic, and at page 12.191, beginning at line 5 through 10, you talked about how at Rambouillet and Paris you'd had some conversations with him, and you said: "And I distinctly remember Mr. Sainovic sitting there thoughtfully and finally responding to my question with words something to the effect that he did not have the authority to be that flexible and that there were too many constraints on him imposed by Belgrade, and at the end of the day there was nothing he could do in this direction, whether he wanted to or not." My question is based on what you knew of the personalities involved -- or who was he referring to when he talked about constraints imposed upon him by Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: My inference at the time was he was -- he was talking about President Milosevic, but that -- that was basically a personal, if you will, speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did he -- and he said there was nothing he could do, whether he wanted to or not. Did he say whether he wanted to?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I -- what I remember is I asked him if he could make a telephone call to Belgrade, and he replied something to the effect that it would no have no affect.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk [Realtime transcript error read as "Cepic"] asked you some questions about the Podujevo incident, and I think beginning at page 12.195, he asked if you or KDOM had received reports about the problems in Podujevo. You said that you had. What action, if any, did you or KDOM take to check out those complaints about the problems in Podujevo in connection with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, there were a number of problems in Podujevo. We talked earlier about the deployment of a VJ battle group to the area. I recall there was also a very serious problem, in that sometime in, I recall, mid-December, a Serbian policeman had been kidnapped by the KLA, I believe, on the outskirts of Podujevo, and on that particular incident General Lukic called me, informed me of the incident, and asked me for my help in getting this fellow, who's name I've forgotten, getting this fellow released. We went into action. We informed KVM. But Walker suggested we go up. And to make a long story short, after very difficult negotiations that spanned several days with Remi and his Deputy-General Dija, we succeeded in obtaining the release of the Serbian policeman, and he was released. And he was released to Bill Walker, who came up for that occasion. The second incident, of course, was the deployment of the VJ battle group, because my deputy, who was a marine lieutenant colonel, and if I may say, he was a marine's marine, he was very impressive, a very good soldier, had lots of experience, he had earned the respect of the KLA, particularly in the Llap zone, because the officer core of the KLA in the Llap zone contained the largest percentage of former VJ and MUP officers of the entire KLA. I learned that later. But in any case, Remi's deputies were all former MUP or VJ officers. There was a rapport there, because -- between Mike Dean, Lieutenant-Colonel Mike Dean, and the KLA officers, they were professionals, so I sent Mike up and he spent a couple of days trying to talk Remi and his people into moving their troops back -- farther back from positions they had taken up along the Pristina-Podujevo-Nis road. It was -- it was clear to any observer who knew the slightest thing about military affairs that the KLA deployment, which the KLA claimed was in response to the VJ battle group's deployment, threatened that road and threatened the rail line which was of strategic importance to Serbia, and our interest was in diffusing a crisis and preventing further conflict. So that was the extent of our engagement in that particular affair.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In connection with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before you move on, the question to which this was a response related to cross-examination, I think, by Mr. Sepenuk and not Mr. Cepic as recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It was Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And following up on that Podujevo incident, Mr. Sepenuk asked you yesterday, I think beginning at page 12.197, line 19, he sort of summed up what you had gone through at that point and he said: "So with the KLA posing a very serious threat to the military and with the rather desperate situation, the civilians in Podujevo, don't you think there's some reasonable basis to say that the actions of the VJ forces fell within that part of the Clark-Naumann Agreement which allowed Serb forces basically to exercise the right of self-defence?" And you agreed that you recognised the right of the Serb security forces to defend themselves. But if, indeed, that's what they were doing in Podujevo, do you know a reason why they would claim that they were just engaging in an exercise?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I suggested yesterday, my own judgment at the time was that they used -- they responded that they were only -- only engaged in an exercise because they must have felt that they were violating the agreement in moving this battle group out of Pristina barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In connection with that, Your Honour, I would like to show the witness Exhibit P-928. This was an exhibit I listed on documents I intended to show the witness, but I didn't show it to him on direct exam. But I think it's pertinent to this point that's been raised on cross-exam. These are the minutes of a VJ Collegium meeting of the main staff on the 30th of December, 1998, and if I'd like to go to page 13, first. And if I could hand a hard copy of the witness -- of pages 13 and 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Mr. Byrnes, this is -- you'll see at the bottom of the page there's a reference to General Dimitrijevic is speaking here, and actually the part I'm interested in is on the following page, page 14, if we can go to page 14, and I've highlighted a portion there. If you could read that out, and then I have a question for you about how that relates to what we're discussing now.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, are you asking me to read it out orally?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Read it out loud for us, please.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: The paragraph begins: "In addition, the current situation in the vicinity of Podujevo, I think we must be completely consistent here and completely open towards each other, so to speak. This situation in Podujevo and the surroundings, it was complex before, but when it did suddenly become -- but when did it suddenly become even more complicated. After the so-called pretend or real-planned exercises in which this company took part in the field. "General, these sorts of moves will lead us to disaster. The explanation that this was a planned exercise, that is not true. It was planned that the unit would provoke the terrorists so that the MUP would then have to do whatever it had to do. The fact that the MUP did not do what it had to do afterwards has resulted in what we have now. "Therefore, this is in addition to everything that General Marijanovic said that we should consider. I think that it is a priority to ensure that not even Sainovic or any other Sainovic can solve these problems by lightly deciding to use the units. The situation has now turned, and that is why we have now been threatened again and all the rest by the -- and we've now been threatened again and all the rest by the International Community, and of course that they blame us for the difficult situation. Instead of dealing with this in another way so that the Siptar side is held responsible, I feel that we should especially keep that part in mind and that we must ensure that the corps commander, and now even the army commander, cannot make such moves while we here are simply informed of what had happened in a roundabout way."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You can stop there. Based on that, is that consistent with your view that this deployment of this company was in violation of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And no one ever asserted to you that they -- at that time that they believed they were acting pursuant to their right under the agreement to engage in self-defence?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly did not. But to be very precise, I was not the official that such -- such comments would have been made to. They would have been made to the KVM officials responsible for -- for ensuring the implementation of the October agreements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, that's fair. I want to move on. Mr. Ackerman, at page 12.188, and Bakrac shortly after, both asked you a couple of brief questions about the conduct of the VJ or the army that you observed, and you described it as generally honourable and professional, I think. My question was: You were not in Kosovo, yourself, between late February and mid-June, '99, were you?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And have you ever seen any of the joint command minutes from 1998 or VJ orders concerning combat activities in '99?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Fila on his feet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpreted] Well, no, but it's too late now, it's too late. I don't understand. What kind of joint command comes out of the cross-examination? So far we've been listening to the prosecutor, who says that we go beyond the examination-in-chief. Who talked about the General Staff, who talked about the record of the VSO? Why is he talking about Sainovic and about things that were never mentioned in the first place? I really protest, Mr. President, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, the reference to Exhibit 928 was made in the context of exploring the nature of the VJ activity around Podujevo, and that is a legitimate matter which does arise out of cross-examination. The reference to Sainovic is an incidental aspect of that, and if you consider it necessary to cross-examine the witness further on that aspect because it's come out in a different context from the one in which you cross-examined initially, then we would allow you to do that. The second point you raise, relating to the joint command minutes, seems to have been resolved in any event, since the witness said that he has not seen any of the joint command minutes. So whether they exist or not and the extent of them is not an issue for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR.  HANNIS
utterances.text: The purpose of my asking those questions, Your Honour, is just to determine the basis for his opinion, what knowledge he had to form that opinion about the VJ's conduct and what he may not have had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to move on to page 12.204, beginning at line 6 through 10. I believe this was Mr. Ivetic was asking you about whether you knew anything about the reputation of General DZ and -- and William Walker among the Serbs, and you said that with regard to Mr. Walker, you had the distinct impression that the Serbs considered him anti-Serb. To your personal knowledge, was he anti-Serb?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I think when Bill Walker arrived in Kosovo, he was not anti-Serb. I think Bill tried his very best, because in particular he had an international mandate to try to stabilise the situation, so a political resolution could be found. He bent over backwards to be -- to be fair and impartial. And I would add to that, that based on my experience with him over the first couple of months, he was -- he was quite frustrated by the KLA. He was quite unhappy with what he saw was provocative KLA behaviour in a number of areas. He had very great difficulty dealing with KLA leadership on specific issues, and I recall particularly the negotiations that led to the release of eight VJ soldiers who stumbled into a KLA encampment, I think, in early January of 1999; he had great difficulty with Commander Remi's stubbornness during the mid or late -- it was around Christmas when the Podujevo -- the deployment of the VJ battle group led to increased tension between the KLA and the Serbian security forces in the Podujevo area and eventually led to actual conflict. Bill had very great -- he was very angry and very frustrated by Remi's stubbornness. He was also frustrated in his dealings with the Serbs, too, particularly over the issue of trying to push that battle group back to barracks. So I think at the outset, he certainly was not anti-Serb, and he certainly bent over backwards to be fair to both parties. And my general impression, by the end of 1998, was, if anything, he was -- he was much more frustrated with the Albanians and felt them more obstructionist.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know, based on your contacts with the KLA members and leaders, whether or not the KLA had an opinion about Walker?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. I'm chuckling because -- it's not funny. Too many people died as a result of this. But in retrospect, it's ironic. The KLA leadership that we dealt with, and on a regular basis, that was Jakup Krasniqi, who was the spokesman, Sokol Bashota, who was a liaison with the internationals, and Rambouillet, who was a member of the political director to their general staff, these three people, who I had over time a great deal of contact with, considered Walker to be pro-Serb. They didn't trust him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The last question I had for you today: Mr. Ivetic asked you about despite having information as to the criminal nature of some of the commanders of the KLA, was there still pressure to downplay the KLA activities, and -- and if not assist them, to put pressure on the Serb authorities? You said, No, there was not, and I would be happy to amplify. Do you recall that question and answer, and do you want to amplify now?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, yeah. I think in the interests of not only history, but in the interests of giving the Court my perspective on what was going on the ground, I would like to amplify. Thank you for giving me the time to do so, and I will try to be as brief as I can. We, at KDOM, were, I'd say, well aware of what I would characterise as criminal activities on the part of some KLA units and some KLA commanders. One of these things -- one of these activities which we dealt on a very regular basis were murders of Serbian civilians and -- and kidnapping of Serbian civilians. This, unfortunately, happened all too regularly. I spent and my team spent an awful lot of time trying to find people, trying to track down Serbian civilians. We did so at General Lukic's request; we did so at Mr. Odalovic's request; we did so on our own. We also, I would add, spent time trying to track down Kosovo-Albanians who disappeared, in particular members, senior members, of Mr. Rugova's LDK party. I can remember on two specific occasions on which the KLA kidnapped these people in the field and held them. In both cases, we were -- in those two instances, we were fortunate and we were able to obtain their release. We were aware there were nasty things going on in the field. Christopher Hill, who was our special envoy, was privy to far more information than we were. KDOM was an unclassified operation. We did not have a secure telephone or a secure telecommunications link. Our communications with Washington were either directly by open telephone or fax. Most of our communications with Washington went by telephone and fax through our embassies at either Belgrade or Skopje. Christopher Hill, as the Ambassador at Estonia, had a secure communications facility and had access to US -- all US diplomatic reporting, classified and otherwise, as well as intelligence. And I -- I remember Chris, on a number of occasions, commenting on how difficult it was for him to deal with what he considered criminals and drug smugglers and all the rest. So he clearly had a much better -- a much bigger picture of alleged KLA criminal activities in a broader sense. That said, I never felt any pressure to play down KLA activities. When we had a number of high-level incidents, we went -- we went to general quarters. It took no instructions from Washington for me to call Krasniqi and complain and remonstrate about an activity that we could assume was the product of a KLA action. And I recall specifically that, I think it was either in late December or early in January, a grenade was thrown into a cafe or billiard room in Pec, the city of Pec in Western Kosovo, a place where young Serbs gathered. A number of them were killed. My recollection is the number was six, but it may have been higher, it may have been lower, but it was a gross event. It was dreadful. And this had occurred shortly after the VJ had ambushed a KLA convoy trying to cross the border with weapons and supplies from Albanian. A number of KLA had been killed. I think it was in the 20s. And the rest of the convoy or group had been captured. The grenade attack in Pec seemed, on the surface, to be a KLA response, but simply because the grenade attack was directed against Serbs, it was hard to believe that Serbs would go and kill other Serbs, particularly in this situation. So our immediate -- my immediate response was to get a hold of Krasniqi and yell at him, you know, What the hell is going on here, and tell him that this kind of stuff had to be stopped. It was not contributing to what everybody professed was our common goal, political resolution. I subsequently received very strong instructions, and Walker did as well, to go in and deal very directly and very forcefully with these people. If I may, I would like to say one other general thing, and these relate to the October agreements. After they were signed, we observed generally a reduction in violent activity by both sides. We entered into, in fact, a period of armed truce. From Belgrade's standpoint, there was a clear interest in satisfying the terms of the agreement. Belgrade wanted international interference in the Kosovo problem to go away, and it wasn't going to go away unless they complied with these international agreements. From the standpoint of the KLA, and it's important to note here that the KLA was not party to these agreements, they didn't sign them, Bill Walker's job and my job and Nick Turnbull, the EU KDOM chief's job, was to go out into the field and sell these agreements to the KLA zone commanders to persuade them to abide by their terms, even though they had not been involved in the negotiations and they'd not signed these agreements. Initially, by and large, the KLA respected the agreements, and they had an interest in respecting it. And we made it very clear, what their interest was. The KLA wanted the International Community in Kosovo -- they wanted us there, and in particular they wanted the United States there. The United States was the big guy on the block. The United States had the most military power in NATO, and so forth and so on. They wanted us there. And it was clear, at least to some of their leadership, that bad behaviour on their part and on the part of their soldiers would risk and put at risk their goal of getting full American and full NATO engagement on their side against the Serbs. So initially, they agreed to stand down. There were -- we never had a perfect situation, but I would say the first two, three, four weeks there were fewer incidents, there were fewer provocations, but it went downhill. Why did it go downhill? In my judgement, neither side trusted each other. The KLA believed that come spring, the Serbs' security forces would launch a new offensive, because the KLA knew KVM had no force. We didn't have tanks, we didn't have guns. There was basically nothing the KDOM could do to stop the Serbs. We had a piece of paper, but if Belgrade decided to violate that, for whatever reason, they would do so. This -- what this speaks to is the lack of trust between the KLA and the Albanians, I would say in general, and Belgrade at that point. On the other hand, I would be dishonest if I did not tell you that the KLA commanders, the KLA leadership, saw the October agreement as an opportunity to regroup and rearm. We were aware of that. We saw the -- in the field, we saw increasing numbers of KLA, and in particular our team saw KLA training camps in the Pagarusa valley, a piece of land in central Kosovo that lay between Malisevo in the north and Suva Reka in the south. We would remonstrate with them, telling this is a clear violation, they were not supposed to be building up under the terms of an agreement that they, of course, hadn't signed, and their response was always, "We know the Serbs are building up. They're smuggling tanks and artillery and more special police into Kosovo behind your backs, and we have to be prepared." KVM had no way of stopping this, other than to go in and bang on the table in Belgrade or Pristina. Ultimately, this led to threats of more NATO intervention. In any case, that's -- that is a -- a hopefully brief recap of what I remember the situation being at the time, and I want to make sure that I've offered a broader picture than some of the more specific answers I offered yesterday did. Thank you, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Byrnes. I don't have any other questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Hannis asked Mr. Byrnes some questions based on the Prosecution Exhibit 928, which is the Collegium of the General Staff for the period December 30, 1998. This was listed as an exhibit by the Prosecution at 65 ter but was not used by them. I think it was used by them very narrowly and unfairly, and I would like Your Honour to -- to request some -- a very brief re-cross-examination on it. It was raised by Mr. Hannis. I think he's presented a very one-sided and twisted and perverted picture, quite frankly, and I would ask for the opportunity to try to set the record straight on this question of -- Mr. Hannis said, No one ever asserted to you at that time that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Is this -- are you now into the question or are you still addressing --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: No, no, still addressing. Maybe I should stop addressing and simply wait for some sort of an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you object to this? You may object to the language used, but do you object to the request for re-cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the entire document is in evidence. The court is free to read the Collegium minutes, but I don't object if he wants to go to some particular point in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The fact that the whole document is in evidence, of course, hasn't stopped you asking questions about it, so presumably the same rule applies to the Defence. And let's deal with the whole issue at this stage. I get the impression Mr. Fila wants to ask further questions also. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Fila, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpreted] I have only one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's hear from Mr. Sepenuk first, then. Please proceed with the additional cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Further cross-examination by Mr. Sepenuk:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, if we could put Prosecution Exhibit 928 up on the screen again, please. And I'm going to refer you specifically to page 7. What I'm going to do, Mr. Byrnes, is ask you about other comments. You read out a particular comment of General Dimitrijevic before in answering Mr. Hannis's question. I just want to put some more of General Dimitrijevic's comments into evidence, and I would ask you to also read these particular portions. So on page 7 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do these, Mr. Sepenuk, relate to the question of whether the business in Podujevo was an exercise or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It relates to the question, Your Honour, of whether the situation -- whether the VJ presence in Podujevo was for the twin purposes of preserving lines of communication and helping out the civilians there, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if you could start with on the top, "As for Kosovo and Metohija," please?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: By the way, I just want to say this General Dimitrijevic. I represent that to you. He's speaking now, please.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I speaking too fast when I read?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if you could read slowly, I'm sure the Trial Chamber and the interpreters would greatly appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: "As for Kosovo and Metohija and the situation in the field, Albanian terrorists continue the activities that we have already mentioned here and which, as a priority, involve reinforcements, consolidating existing and forming new complements and staffs, and obtaining new weapons. These activities are especially apparent in the area of Llap.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can you just stop there? In other words, in the Podujevo area; correct?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Llap? Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Where they are anyway -- where they are anyway where the situation is most critical, and where these hundred or so Serbs find themselves practically surrounded. So at this point, the situation is very volatile" --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, you skipped a -- go ahead, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: "So at this point, the situation is very volatile and the situation has become even more complex after one of our units carried out exercises in the area."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. Now, would you please go to page 8? This is again General Dimitrijevic speaking. First paragraph, and read just that first paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beginning with "Increasing"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The increasing number of terrorist acts against Serbs is a special danger at the moment, as the intent is to intimidate them and encourage them to move out of Kosovo and Metohija, as well as to bring terrorist activities into urban areas. At this moment, this occurs most frequently in the area of Podujevo where the Serbian villages of Obrandza, Peranej [phoen] and Velika Krusa have almost -- have almost -- have been almost completely abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And now again General Dimitrijevic speaking. If we could go to page 10, and down at the bottom of the page starting with the paragraph: "The overall safety ..." Come up, please. Scroll up, please. Yes, that paragraph starting: "The overall safety," and that is again General Dimitrijevic speaking. Do you see it there, sir?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you mind please reading that?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The overall safety of these remaining hundred or so Serbs who find themselves, as I've already said, completely surrounded. So what is actually keeping the situation from getting out of control is our company there. The MUP has moved, and the company could really find itself in a very unpleasant situation of being attacked by these terrorist forces, which are numerically much stronger than -- than -- which are numerically much stronger than it. "To be honest, I fear that if all this comes down again to the army having to ensure the functioning of the system -- to the army having to ensure that Serbs remain, to the army having to ensure their safety, I fear that we will not be successful."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Please stop there. And then finally would you go to page 17? You see where it says: "These claims presented here ..." at the top, and with the Court's indulgence, I can read that because this is not General Dimitrijevic. Everything you've been reading to this point is General Dimitrijevic. This is General Ojdanic. And if you can just read along with me to make sure I'm reading it correctly, General Ojdanic says: "These claims presented here regarding the situation down there in around Podujevo that the presence of this unit added to it, it was really a matter of whether the marching route and the location of the camp were selected correctly, but this unit really was bivouacked there. I was assured of this by the commander of the army, but at one time General Perisic said, when he agreed to the condition of withdrawal, that if they did not ensure what was expected of them, so if the other side continues to be active -- so if the other side continues to be active and threatens the Serbian population, we would be forced to bring this group back into this area." Did I read that correctly, Mr. Byrnes?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then, Your Honour, just one more matter, and that is Prosecution Exhibit 414. I did refer to it briefly yesterday. This was the letter from the two gentlemen who were members of the Podujevo Municipal Assembly talking about how Serb -- Serb civilians in the Podujevo area had been threatened by the KLA, including the KLA in those black uniforms - we had some testimony about the secret police of the KLA - and again on this question of safety and the request of the Podujevo national assembly to bring in the VJ, I would like to have just two -- two passages from this letter read, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How does that arise out of Mr. Hannis's re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Well, it's on the point of the twin purposes for having the VJ there, i.e., to secure the lines of communication and to protect the civilians, and that it was the civilians who were besieging, exhorting, the Serb military and Serb security forces to come to the area and help them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are limits to the extent to which rules may be relaxed in this situation, and you've already -- and all you've done so far, Mr. Sepenuk, you failed to ask a question, and Mr. Hannis has been proved to be right, that all that you wanted to do can be done by reading the document, which is already part of the evidence in the case. So what has happened so far as a result of the Chamber's indulgence is really a waste of time. So let us think about what you now say in relation to Exhibit 414 before we give our ruling on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're satisfied that we can read Exhibit P-414 for ourselves and that there's no need for any further cross-examination on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, what was your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same thing you allowed me last time when I protested. Further cross-examination by Mr. Fila:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, the document that was read out to you by Mr. Hannis and Mr. Sepenuk, have you ever seen it before, the collegium minutes? Have you ever seen it before today?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Therefore, do you know anything about Sainovic's role concerning this company in Podujevo or any such thing?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, I have a vague recollection that Bill Walker dealt with Mr. Sainovic in an effort to diffuse what we saw as a crisis situation, and -- but that is the extent of my knowledge of what Mr. Sainovic's role would have been with regard to this specific incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason for my protest was that the entire collegium minutes talk about Podujevo, and Mr. Hannis found it necessary to read out only the portion mentioning Mr. Sainovic, where -- and all the generals were mentioning in Podujevo and talking at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question, certainly speaking for myself, appears to have been perfectly justified, Mr. Fila, but you should also be reminded that the whole document will be considered in the context of our deliberations. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one matter I would like to ask the witness about. It's very brief. It would require us going into private session, but I think it responds to Mr. Hannis' question regarding that portion of Exhibit, I think 928, dealing with what was a kind of alleged irresponsibility on the part of the VJ. And I can't tell you more about it in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it, it extends to more than simply a recitation of what was in the document that's part of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with a document that's part of the evidence. You won't be able to read it unless I bring it to your attention?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but you say it has a bearing on what was said in Exhibit 928?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it has an indirect bearing on that because I think the force of what Mr. Hannis was trying to accomplish was to show an irresponsibility toward the Holbrooke-Milosovic agreement on the part of the VJ, and I think this deals directly with that and it actually is information that comes directly from this witness; not from any other source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, what do you have to say on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't object, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we need to go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Further cross-examination by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, you were interviewed in Zagreb on the 5th and 6th of February 2001 by a person named Shin and a person named Philip Coo from the Tribunal. Do you remember that interview?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The quickest way for us to do this is for me to simply read to you a little section from that interview and just ask you if you can confirm that was your -- I think it may refresh your memory a bit, and just ask you to confirm it? What the report says is that: "Byrnes was convinced that the Serbs' security forces had excellent intelligence on the KLA through signals, intercepts, penetration of the KLA by agents, informers, and other sources. Once, shortly after the GJ agreement, Lukic showed Byrnes a vast map on the wall of a large conference room next to his office in the MUP building. The map was marked with all known KLA positions. Pavkovic was similarly well informed. On several occasions, Pavkovic told Byrnes where to find KLA personnel or headquarters when Byrnes needed to find such persons. Such information often compromised very specific information. In one case, even identifying the exact house where someone Byrnes was looking for would be. Byrnes was perplexed by the fact that despite having such good intelligence, the Serb forces did not act on it by attacking KLA headquarters and other locations occupied by key personnel." First of all, does that refresh your memory to any extent?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say you were perplexed by the fact they didn't attack, I think -- would it be fair to say what you were saying is you were surprised when they had that much knowledge about where these headquarters and these people were, that they used the restraint that they used?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was indeed, because I assumed standard military doctrine is to try to destroy, if you will, the head of your enemy. If you can take out its leadership, you significantly weaken its ability to fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Anything arising, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Just one in connection with that. I think--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do we stay in private session and is it on the last matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, well, because it relates to the source of where it comes from. Further re-examination by Mr. Hannis:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, now that you say your memory is refreshed partly by hearing that, from that it sounds like you actually met with General Pavkovic on more than one occasion. And I believe you testified earlier that you only met with him once. Having had your memory refreshed, are you satisfied now that you must have met with him on more than one occasion, to the extent it says "on several occasions, Pavkovic told Byrnes where to find KLA personnel."

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am very convinced that I met General Pavkovic only on one occasion and that was in his headquarters in Pristina shortly after the signing of the Jovanovic/Geremek understanding, accord. What I think is -- I think this is a mistake, if you will, on the part of the investigators. I think -- in reading this, I think they confused a conversation I had with General Lukic with conversations that they thought I had with Pavkovic. To repeat, I do not remember seeing General Pavkovic more than once, and I never had a conversation with him -- I never had a one-on-one conversation with General Pavkovic particularly about such things as this. If I may, I would like to recap the incident because I've never forgotten it. It was shortly after the signing of the agreements, and I was directed -- EU and US KDOM in their capacities as stand-ins for KVM, which hadn't stood up yet, we were asked, as I said earlier, to explain and hopefully sell the agreement to the KLA in the field, and we were particularly asked to try to push the KLA from roads in the Malisevo area and off the Podujevo-Pristina-Nis highway. I went in to see General Lukic, who was very much aware of this, but to explain to him what Nick Turnbull and I were going to try to do, and I remember asking him, Where do I -- do you know where I can find the Llap zone leadership, Mr. Remi? We did not have much of a relationship with those people. And at which point I recall he took me from his office around the corner into his conference room where there was a very large wall map, a very detailed wall map of Kosovo, and he went up to it and put his finger on a village, whose name I don't remember, and actually to a house that had little black dots indicating houses, and the larger dots indicating, for example, schools or municipal buildings, and he said, You will find him in this compound. It was extraordinary. I was really amazed that he had such knowledge. Well, we mounted up -- we made a call to one of the KLA we knew in the area and told him we were coming up to see Remi, and that's exactly where they took us. They took us to the house that General Lukic had indicated with his finger on the map. I've never forgotten that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So then to clarify, it wasn't Pavkovic who told you on several times locations?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never had a conversation with Pavkovic, and I would like to reiterate, unless my memory has really failed me, I never had a one-on-one personal conversation with General Pavkovic. I might well have liked to, but I never had such an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So who was it then that gave you this information?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Lukic gave me this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say "gave you that information," do you extend that answer beyond the occasion when he showed you the vast map to several occasions?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. General Lukic and I had numerous conversations about the KLA, about their operating tactics, where they were, their -- their structure, their weaponry, and on several occasions he indicated to me a very considerable knowledge of the KLA and its organisational structure, but not -- however, not down to that -- the level of specificity that he indicated on this one occasion I just related.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The note that's been made, Mr. Byrnes, said: "On several occasions Pavkovic," and we know that you think that's wrong, but it says: "Pavkovic told Byrnes where the KLA or headquarters were when Byrnes needed to find such persons." Is that an accurate statement of what Lukic did or should we disregard that part of your note, of the note that's been made of your interview?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's inaccurate in the sense that, in my memory, General Lukic on only one occasion provided such information related to the location of a specific KLA officer, on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have just two questions, real brief, based on Mr. Lukic being -- showing the map. I know we're well long over the break, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think we'll have the break just now. I take it you don't object to that being explored, in view of the way the evidence has developed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we do need to have the break at this stage, Mr. Byrnes, so we'll resume at 20 -- sorry, at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll try to be brief. Further cross-examination by Mr. Ivetic:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, I just wanted to clarify the item that you've just testified about, since I know much time has passed and, as you've said several times, your memory, as anyone's, could be fuzzy relating to specific events. Relating to this incident that you said was where Mr. Lukic showed you where to find Remi, do you perhaps recall and does it refresh your recollection if I remind you that there was an incident where two police officers from Kosovo Polje had been kidnapped, and you had met with the family members of the kidnapped police officers and had promised to try and obtain their release from the KLA and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Ivetic. It was probably premature on my part to suggest that we could return to open session. Should this, Mr. Hannis, remain in private session? I was, in fact, going to ask if any of it actually needed to remain private session material when we finished, and it was premature in letting the cross-examination proceed in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I guess this should be, in light of what we did with the other stuff that comes from his statement, which is subject to the protective measure, and then at the end of the day we can look at all of it and see whether all or some of it can be open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we shall return to private session. And I'm sorry about this confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I should have also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, it's my mistake, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps you should start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, again to try and refresh your recollection as to this event, do you recall an instance if I remind you that there was an incident where two police officers from Kosovo Polje had been kidnapped by the KLA, and you had met with the family members of these policemen who had pleaded for you to intervene, and you had promised that you would do so, and that in fact the building in question that had been identified was in the village of Likovac in the Drenica region, near Glinovac [phoen] municipality, where these kidnapped Serbian police officers were being held by the KLA, and, in fact, the reason that Mr. Lukic knew the appearance of the building so down to detail was that it was a former police station of the Serbian MUP that had been taken over, and that the police had been ejected from when the KLA took over that area. Does that refresh your recollection as to this event that you have just testified to relating to the map and the location of the house, I believe a two-storey house with some figures of animals on the second floor?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you could help me a bit. Do you, by any chance, have a date? I have a vague, vague recollection of part of this, but if you had a date, it might help.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me see if I can obtain a date, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is this a reference to the black -- to the large map incident? It's the occasion of you being shown a large map that you've described to us already, and Mr. Ivetic is trying to connect that, link that, to the particular circumstances he's just described here.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- what I remember is that General Lukic showed me the specific location of Commander Remi and his staff in the Podujevo area on the large map. He used the large map, as I recall, to talk generally about KLA or even police deployments in Kosovo more broadly, but I don't have any memory of General Lukic, on another occasion, using that map to point out the specific location of where somebody might be held. I hope I'm clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've given evidence of being told the exact location of where KLA personnel could be located, and being told that by General Lukic, and I certainly had an impression that that may have happened in the context of viewing this large map. But is that my misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Lukic -- what I recall is that General Lukic used this large map, it was probably early November, 1998, to pinpoint the location of Remi and his staff in the Podujevo area. With respect to the incident that Mr. Ivetic is asking about now, that is a totally separate incident. Likovac is in Drenica in central Kosovo perhaps a hundred kilometres away from Podujevo. I hope that clarifies my response.
