utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that clarification. No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nothing further, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have a question, more of a query. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Now, while answering a question which was from Mr. Hannis's side, you answered that, yes, you suggested to Mr. Sainovic that he picked up the telephone and rang up Belgrade at the relevant time, and the reply was, "It will have no effect." While doing so, you went into -- you had a deep breath, rather it appeared that you sighed, and that sigh looked, of course, painful. Now, I was astonished what would be behind that, what obsessed you at the relevant moment, and I thought this -- I may request you to kindly tell us on that before I ask another question. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that -- that conversation with Mr. Sainovic took place at the very -- the very last day of the Paris conference, sometime -- I think the conference broke up on March 13th or March 15th. It was the very last day and it was literally the last hour before the conference broke up. I -- as I said earlier, I knew that the NATO threat was not a bluff, and I knew that if we didn't get an agreement, that we would have more conflict, and that meant -- that meant more deaths. And we'd seen -- we'd seen quite enough of that, not only in Kosovo but we'd seen quite a bit of it in Croatia and Bosnia before. And I thought that anything we could do even at that moment to try to head that off and to provide another opportunity to find a political solution would save lives. I saw -- I saw plenty of bodies in Kosovo. I dealt with plenty of people on both sides who lost family members and friends. I didn't want to see any more of that. That was -- that was a personal moral feeling. But I was also under instructions from the very beginning, as were my colleagues, to do everything possible to stabilise the situation, to prevent more conflict, and to give the diplomats and statesmen a chance to work out something that would be acceptable to both sides and save -- and save lives. I mean, we were talking about the little people on both sides, the Serb civilians and the Albanians. I mean, I had -- I had no illusions about what would happen. There were -- there were people on both sides who were eager to pull the trigger, and as we had seen particularly in the fall of 1998, both sides had not refrained from what I considered, and I think it was a universal consideration -- neither side had shrunk from very grievous human rights violations. I mean, I was there. I saw villages that had been burned, I saw the effect on mothers and children on both sides. I developed very close relationship with a couple of Kosovo-Polje-Serb families whose husbands had been kidnapped and had -- as far as I know, they have never returned. And I was pretty confident at the time that they had been killed. One family, in particular, lost a husband near Velika Hoca, near Rakovac, that -- and he left a wife and two young boys with no source of income. I just didn't want to see any more of that. I thought anything we could do to stop anything, it was worth it. We were again talking about lives. So that's -- that's the only way I can answer your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you. The second question was that: You talked organising the role of the Yugoslav Army vis-a-vis other persons with whom they had interaction, and one such group was your men, as you said, and you said that they were very nicely treated, and rather one of them was rescued. Now, I just wanted to ask whether this was for only your men or was it for others; I mean, all and sundry? And is it because your men were identifiable because they were wearing uniforms or some particular dress, that they could be distinguished from the rest, and they were shown -- they were given care and they were shown special concern. Is it that -- did your people wear a uniform or was it just general? That, I thought, was another question which is a clarification. Thank you very much, and I have one more question.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. As I understand your question, it relates to the treatment of US KDOM personnel by Yugoslav Army VJ personnel. That's correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. First, we did not wear uniforms. Our standard uniform was, depending on the weather, a sports shirt and jeans or I wore chinos, kaki trousers. And the military -- US military officers who were assigned to the mission were under strict instructions not to wear uniforms. I don't think any of them even had a uniform with them in their kit. However, our vehicles were very clearly marked. Initially, we had British Land Rovers and Chevrolet Suburbans, which you may be familiar with, it's a large van. And on the sides -- on the sides of the vehicles, we had US flags, EU KDOM had the EU flag. These flags were also on the top of the vehicle in the event there were aircraft in the area. Because we had a couple of instances in which our Land Rovers were either fired on or nearly fired on by KLA, we decided to paint our vehicles a very distinctive colour. And let me backtrack for a moment. The Serbian police also had the same type of Land Rover we had, and in -- at dusk -- at dusk or when light -- light was bad, the KLA, which of course was very nervous, would on occasion -- our judgment was they had confused one of our Land Rovers with a Serbian police vehicle. So to avoid that sort of problem in the future, we painted our vehicles a -- a luminescent orange. We were, in some cases, the laughing stock of the province, but we actually asked our experts back in Washington for the best, most luminous colour day or night, and that's what they came back with. So you had -- at the end of the day when KVM was set up, you might have had something in the neighbourhood of 200 various types of vehicles painted this ludicrous luminous orange running around the province. One final point. After KVM was set up, the US military gave us about 20 armoured Humvees, the standard-issue US military jeep, and there was no other vehicle like that in the province, so it was perfectly clear from even a distance to anybody who -- who we were. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think there must be some Dutch-American there suggesting your orange. Anyway, my last question would be that you wanted to speak to Krasniqi about -- if I'm not correctly pronouncing the name, forgive me. Krasniqi or Krasnici?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Krasniqi. Did you ever speak to him? Or you were only contemplating, because you thought that nasty things were going on, these are your words, and you referred this to the activities of a concerned group, and you wanted to speak to him. Did you speak to him, and if you did speak to him, how did he react? What was his response? And I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I spoke to Jakup Krasniqi on many, many, many occasions, both directly and using a satellite telephone. Were you -- was your request -- was your question related to a very specific incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Now, as you have elucidated, as you have explained further, I would say that what type of response he had, whenever you whimpered about those nasty things you were talking of while answering questions here, please. Or what were you talking to him then otherwise?

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krasniqi, if I may -- if I may elaborate a bit, Jakup Krasniqi was the spokesman for the KLA. Normally, when we -- we and by -- let me use the broad "we." We, KDOM, or EU KDOM or KVM, normally when we met at, let's say, a high level with the KLA leadership, we met with a troika of the KLA officials, and that troika consisted normally of Jakup Krasniqi; a man named Ram Buja, who was a member of the political directorate of the KLA; and then this Sokol Bashota, who was a member of the General Staff and was the -- the liaison -- the General Staff's liaison officer with the internationals, not just US KDOM but all the internationals. So when we met with them ourselves or when we took -- as we did quite frequently, we took official visitors out to meet with the KLA leadership. Official visitors like, for example, Ambassadors Petrisch, Ambassadors Hill, the Kosova working group director of the Department of State, Ambassador Bardo came out once, Larry Rossin, who was a Balkans director at the Department of State came out once, several senators, so -- the contact group ambassadors from Belgrade. We would shuttle these people out to meet the KLA leadership, and that leadership was almost always Krasniqi, Buja and Anne Bashota. As my discussions suggest with these people we talked about a wide range of issues and primarily, of course, trying to find ways to achieve a political solution to the problem. Krasniqi was always the primary speaker. The others would talk, but Krasniqi was, if you will, the KLA point man in these discussions. He was our -- our direct interlocutor. When we had problems, kidnappings, grenade attacks such as the one I described in Pec, incidents such as the deployment of the VJ battle group, or our efforts to arrange a truce, if you will, a ceasefire on the ground in -- in and around Malisevo, Krasniqi was the guy I went to. He seemed to have the most authority, the most responsibility. He seemed to have some -- some ability to make decisions. So, for example, in the Pec -- the bombing of the Serbian cafe in Pec, he was the man I went to, and he was the man, you know, I banged on the table with. I mean, Krasniqi and I had some very testy conversations over -- over the course of this sort of thing, and with respect to the Pec incident, which is the one I think your question was directly referring to, I recall that Krasniqi's response was to deny that that had been done by KLA elements and to suggest at the same time, and I have a distinct memory of this, he suggested that -- and his words were something to the effect, There are -- there is another Albanian armed force in the Pec area which calls itself KLA, but it is not. It goes by the name of FARK. FARK -- FARK was another armed Albanian element, and he blamed that particular incident on the FARK. I hope -- I hope that's an adequate answer, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But what was your general views about this group of three, the troika, whom you met? I mean, how did you find them generally when you talked to them, complaining? They, of course, had an excuse and all that, but how did you find them, generally, because you did mention of others while in your discourse. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SHAUN BYRNES [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the relationship between all of us developed over time. Initially, it was -- they were quite stand-offish and quite reserved. As we got to know one another and as we worked through problems, the relationship became, if you will, became warmer. We -- we respected, I think -- we respected one another. I mean, to be fair, we got some things worked out, but I remember -- if I can give you an anecdote, I can remember at the time when the -- the eight VJ soldiers stumbled into this KLA encampment north of Mitrovica, and General Lukic, I believe, asked me to go out and see the KLA to start working on getting their release, and I remember going out to see them, and it was in the middle of the night, and we had a conversation -- we had a very, shall we say, vigorous and testy conversation. At the end of which Krasniqi got up, and I thought he was going to throw a book at me, and stomped out and said he was never going to deal with me again and this sort of thing, that this was not the KLA's fault, these guys had stumbled in, and they were not going to turn them over, yada-yada-ya, and he stomped out, and I just sat there and I waited for several hours. Bashota was with him. Bashota sat there with me and said, Look, he'll come back, don't worry, he's really -- and he did, and we got -- we continued the conversation. But it took several days of this to even get them to sit down with the people who ultimately resolved the issue on the international side, and that was Ambassador Petrisch, the Austrian Ambassador to Belgrade, and Chris Hill, our special envoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Byrnes, that completes your examination. I hope you feel you've been able to deal with all the issues that you ought to, in light of the questions asked. Thank you very much for coming to the Tribunal to give evidence. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I hope I've been of some assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We can now return to open session, I think. And just before you leave us, the same arrangement should apply as last time. We should review the transcript and the Prosecution will advise the Court and other parties and the registry of those parts that need to remain confidential, and that should be done no later than a week on Friday, which is the 27th. By Friday the 27th. Thank you very much for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MANNING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, we fixed a hearing for Thursday into your application under Rule 54 bis, and one of the responses to that application is that any decision would be premature because General Clark is not on the witness list. We are inclined to postpone that hearing and resume again on Tuesday of next week, in the hope that the position has been clarified by then. Do you have anything to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I completely agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no position on it. I know I spoke with Ms. Schildge yesterday, who was preparing for this week's hearing, but based on that conversation, I suppose she would not have an objection to a delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. O'Sullivan, the position so far as the witness Lilic is concerned is also dependent on the appeal, to at least some extent, and therefore we are inclined to think that a decision on that should also be postponed. And hopefully, it can be dealt with on Tuesday. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I can state our position on the Prosecution's request to have you vary the order, and we strongly oppose that, strongly oppose that. We urge you to enforce your order of the 23rd of March. And if you like, I can tell you why. Because it's all about time frame in preparation of our defences, and harmonising our defences, and getting out in the field and doing our work, and not to be in limbo this week and limbo the week after and the week after that. We saw your order of the 23rd of March precisely to have us to know that this week these two potential witnesses would be here, we would break pending Clark or not, and in the interim we would be out doing our work. And our work of course two things. Our undertaking to the Chamber is that we would seriously work to refine our cases and to coordinate our cases, and those are two very different things and both require time and consultation among ourselves and with our clients. Now, we're paying the price because of what the Prosecution wants you to amend, we're paying the price on having adequate time to prepare a full and coherent defence, coherent for us individually and collectively, and also for the Chamber, to assist you in the clear and efficient presentation of our evidence. Now, we're paying the price for this for the Prosecution not calling its witnesses on time, these last two, especially Lilic. They've known since July that they wanted him, they've known for years they want him, and now here we are having to sit in this city and come back next week or remain here, or have our teams broken up and not to work efficiently. And this is fundamentally unfair to us, and we urge you not to allow this to happen, to enforce your order and leave us knowing that the only potential witness left is General Clark, contingent on the Appeals Chamber decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, you will appreciate that the submission you make has sympathy, and no more so than from myself. However, we also have to be, I think, practical and realistic when the prospect of an important witness being brought is such that he could be heard fairly soon. So there are significant issues to be determined here, and complicating the determination are paragraphs C, D and E of Part 9 of the order that we made on the 23rd of March. So we have decided that we will not make a final decision on the question raised until a motion is actually made by the Prosecution, and we anticipate that that will not be until the outcome of the appeal is known, or at least until the point at which the witness is either available or the outcome of the appeal is known, because it's obviously a possibility that this appeal will take even longer to be determined. The earliest date on which it will be determined, I understand now, is this Friday, but that's not a certainty by any means. So we will postpone a decision on this. We will, however, also consider the impact that any decision to allow his evidence to be heard has on the preparation of the Defence case, and we will consider more detailed submissions on that and recognise the possibility, at least, that the issues that concern you can be resolved in a different way. Now, in the hope that the position may be clear on Friday, but nevertheless to ensure that there is time to relay any change in the arrangements should that not be the case, we propose not sitting until Tuesday of next week. We will therefore fix the next hearing at this stage for -- is it Tuesday morning -- Tuesday at 9.00. If that has to be changed for any reason, then that may happen by e-mail, but what will not happen is the advancement of that. So you can rely on the further sitting of the Trial Chamber being no earlier than Tuesday at 9.00. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Maybe to end the day on a more mundane, routine note, we all have our exhibits that we obsess about. With Mr. Fila, it's 2D8 that he loses sleep about, and mine is Prosecution Exhibit 414. And Your Honour mentioned when you stated that you did not want me to cross-examine any more about it, you said on the record that, You can read 414 for yourselves, and I hope that's going to be true, Your Honour. There's one difficulty here, though. This exhibit has not been officially and formally admitted into evidence. I was allowed to read a paragraph by you to see if it jived with Mr. Byrnes' recollection. I had intended to do that with Mr. Byrnes, again with 414, to see if it jives with his recollection, but quite frankly given the tenor of Your Honour's ruling on my reading, I didn't think this was the appropriate time to do that. But I've since spoken to Mr. Hannis, and I think it's fair to say that he does agree to the admission of this particular exhibit, so that indeed you can read all of the information contained therein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you for that, and P-414 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And then my last question, Your Honour, is: Is it possible that 9.00 Tuesday morning, given there's, let's say, a favourable decision of the Prosecution and Clark, would 9.00 Tuesday morning be the time for General Ojdanic to present his argument on his Rule 54 motion? Is that what you're contemplating?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I think that we will postpone the 54 bis hearing until Tuesday and hope it can proceed then and parties will be prepared to deal with it, and since that doesn't involve the other parties, obviously they do not need to be present in court. However, there may be other -- in fact, there will likely be other issues to be dealt with on Tuesday, so everyone -- all accused will be present in the building and able to be brought into court at whatever stage it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we'll adjourn the trial until Tuesday and also the 54 bis hearing until Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
